children: By Laura Saunders
The great obstacle to effective tax planning for retirement funds is Congress. To make smart moves, savers need to know about future taxes-but this is impossible.
Will lawmakers tackle $40 trillion of debt by raising rates, altering provisions or adding a consumption tax? Maybe, maybe not.

In addition, savers need to predict their own tax rates on retirement-fund withdrawals. How long will you work, and how much will you save? Will your income in retirement fall or rise? These are also hard questions.
The upshot is that tax planning for retirement accounts comes down to guesses.

No wonder the last Tax Report hit a nerve with readers. It delved into the problems affluent savers face when their retirement dollars are concentrated in traditional IRA/401(k) accounts. Required withdrawals can shower these savers with unneeded income that raises tax rates, reduces tax breaks and triggers tax increases.

The column inspired hundreds of reader responses. Some derided these savers for whining about good fortune: "My steak is too juicy and my lobster is too buttery." More were grateful for the column's focus on a widespread issue. Said one, "I wish I had read this 20 years ago."
Readers also raised issues that there wasn't enough space to tackle-so let's keep going.

"Tax planning for retirement involves guesses, but it's important to make smart guesses. A lot of money is at stake," says Edward McQuarrie, a professor emeritus at Santa Clara University who studies retirement strategies.
To cope with an unknown future, savers should try to diversify among traditional IRAs/401(k)s, Roth IRAs/401(k)s and-in some cases-taxable brokerage accounts, as described in the prior column.

Ideally, this would mean savers put after-tax dollars into Roth IRAs/401(k)s when their tax rates are low and then get tax deductions for contributions to traditional IRAs/401(k)s in higher earning years. (Always get the employer match, however.) The goal is to minimize total taxes on savings in retirement accounts.

This strategy wasn't available to current mid- and late-career savers who didn't have access to Roth accounts when young, however. For these savers, McQuarrie warns against adding one problem to another by "overpaying" for Roth contributions and conversions that incur taxes at rates the saver likely won't encounter on withdrawals unless tax rates soar.

Here's a simplified example: John's top tax rate is 22% and could be 22% when he withdraws from retirement accounts. If a Roth IRA conversion is large enough that he would owe taxes on it at a 32% rate, says McQuarrie, he should think about skipping the conversion unless he's convinced his tax rate on withdrawals will go way up.

On the other hand, say John retires and has low-income years that land him in a 12% bracket before he starts required withdrawals at age 73 or 75 (depending on birth year). At those tax rates, Roth IRA conversions could be smart.
But who knows, really? Here are responses to questions readers asked on this topic.
What happens if I do a large Roth IRA conversion and the market crashes?

After years of rising markets, here's food for thought: Owners of traditional IRAs/401(k)s in a way share their losses with Uncle Sam. If the value of the account tanks, the tax on withdrawals will be lower as well, says Ed Slott, a CPA who is an IRA specialist.

With a Roth IRA, that's not the case. Contributions are in after-tax dollars, so tax is paid up front. If the value of the account declines, the losses aren't shared with Uncle Sam when there are withdrawals. "Always try to leave funds in Roth IRAs as long as possible," says Slott.
I'm already taking required withdrawals from my traditional IRA. Can I do Roth conversions?

Yes. The problem is that these payouts, known as RMDs, can't be part of a conversion amount and must be withdrawn first. This will boost the cost of conversions. On the other hand, such conversions could make sense if the owner plans to leave the Roth IRA to a spouse, and the spouse plans to leave it to heirs.
I have a large traditional IRA. Should I do my charitable giving with it?

Yes, almost certainly. In 2026, IRA owners who are at least 701/2 can make Qualified Charitable Distributions, or QCDs, up to a total of $111,000 directly to charities. The donations can count against the giver's RMDs (if any), and QCDs don't raise adjusted gross income that triggers other taxes. This is a highly tax-efficient move for charitably inclined savers.
I'm thinking of doing Roth conversions so my spouse won't owe the "widow's penalty" of higher tax rates if I die. Is this a good idea?
Specialists are divided. The issue is that after one spouse's death, the survivor must switch to "single" filing status, and that can push the survivor into higher tax brackets.

Slott thinks that in many cases, the widow's penalty is a good reason to do a Roth IRA conversion, especially on the final joint return. McQuarrie thinks that in most cases it's not. What's clear is that if there are other reasons to do Roth conversions, the widow's penalty issue doesn't negate them.
I expect to leave traditional IRAs to my heirs. Should I convert them to Roth IRAs?

Most non-spouse heirs of traditional IRAs have 10 years to withdraw the funds, and some must take annual RMDs during that period. To simplify inheritances, many IRA owners like to leave tax-free Roth accounts to their heirs, giving them up to 10 years to withdraw the Roth funds with no required payouts.
I have a large traditional IRA, and I don't have long-term care insurance. Should I do Roth conversions?

Be careful: Long-term care costs are often deductible above a threshold of 7.5% of adjusted gross income. Given the high cost of such care, these deductions can provide substantial tax breaks to those with taxable income.

Because Roth IRA conversions reduce the balance in the owner's traditional IRAs, there are fewer taxable IRA funds available for withdrawal to pay expenses that are deductible. As a result, planners typically recommend keeping enough in traditional IRAs to pay such expenses and get a deduction.
